claim: Collateral sensitivity (CS) occurs when the acquisition of resistance to one antibiotic produces increased susceptibility to a second antibiotic.
source: CS occurs when the acquisition of resistance to one antibiotic produces increased susceptibility to a second antibiotic.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citation to foundational work (Szybalski and Bryson, 1952) in the manuscript.

claim: CS can be exploited for the design of multi-drug strategies that select against antibiotic resistance.
source: CS occurs when the acquisition of resistance to one antibiotic causes increased susceptibility to a second antibiotic (Szybalski and Bryson, 1952) and can be exploited for the design of multi-drug strategies that select against ABR (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Lázár et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating this application.

claim: The development of resistance might be prevented by treatments based on the sequential cycling of antibiotics whose resistance mechanisms produce reciprocal CS.
source: Moreover, recent evidence suggests that the development of resistance might be prevented by treatments based on the sequential cycling of antibiotics whose resistance mechanisms produce reciprocal CS (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and characterized as speculative ('suggests').

claim: Several studies have cataloged CS networks emerging from mutations in chromosomal genes.
source: Several studies have cataloged CS networks emerging from mutations in chromosomal (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Lázár et al., 2013; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Podnecky et al., 2018; Roemhild et al., 2020) and plasmid genes (Dortet et al., 2015; Fröhlich et al., 2019; Rosenkilde et al., 2019), but the CS effects produced by the horizontal acquisition of ABR plasmids remain poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Several studies have cataloged CS networks emerging from mutations in plasmid genes.
source: Several studies have cataloged CS networks emerging from mutations in chromosomal (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Lázár et al., 2013; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Podnecky et al., 2018; Roemhild et al., 2020) and plasmid genes (Dortet et al., 2015; Fröhlich et al., 2019; Rosenkilde et al., 2019), but the CS effects produced by the horizontal acquisition of ABR plasmids remain poorly understood.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The CS effects produced by the horizontal acquisition of ABR plasmids remain poorly understood.
source: Several studies have cataloged CS networks emerging from mutations in chromosomal (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Lázár et al., 2013; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Podnecky et al., 2018; Roemhild et al., 2020) and plasmid genes (Dortet et al., 2015; Fröhlich et al., 2019; Rosenkilde et al., 2019), but the CS effects produced by the horizontal acquisition of ABR plasmids remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap statement based on review of existing literature.

claim: Mobile genetic elements, especially plasmids, play a crucial role in the dissemination of ABR genes between clinical pathogens.
source: Mobile genetic elements, especially plasmids, play a crucial role in the dissemination of ABR genes between clinical pathogens and are one of the major drivers of the alarming worldwide rise in ABR (Partridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Plasmids are one of the major drivers of the alarming worldwide rise in antibiotic resistance.
source: Mobile genetic elements, especially plasmids, play a crucial role in the dissemination of ABR genes between clinical pathogens and are one of the major drivers of the alarming worldwide rise in ABR (Partridge et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Plasmid acquisition tends to produce common metabolic alterations in the host bacterium.
source: Despite the evolutionary advantage conferred by plasmids in the presence of antibiotics, plasmid acquisition tends to produce common metabolic alterations in the host bacterium (San Millan et al., 2018), that typically translate into a fitness cost (San Millan and MacLean, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Metabolic alterations produced by plasmid acquisition typically translate into a fitness cost.
source: Despite the evolutionary advantage conferred by plasmids in the presence of antibiotics, plasmid acquisition tends to produce common metabolic alterations in the host bacterium (San Millan et al., 2018), that typically translate into a fitness cost (San Millan and MacLean, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Six natural plasmids carrying clinically relevant ABR genes were analyzed for collateral effects in Escherichia coli MG1655.
source: To test this hypothesis, we analyzed the collateral effects associated with the acquisition of six natural plasmids carrying clinically relevant ABR genes in Escherichia coli MG1655.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: Most ABR plasmids produce CS events of moderate effect.
source: Our results reveal that most ABR plasmids, including the clinically important carbapenem-resistance conjugative plasmid pOXA-48, produce CS events of moderate effect.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from the study.

claim: The carbapenem-resistance conjugative plasmid pOXA-48 produces CS events of moderate effect.
source: Our results reveal that most ABR plasmids, including the clinically important carbapenem-resistance conjugative plasmid pOXA-48, produce CS events of moderate effect.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: CS responses associated with pOXA-48 can be exploited to preferentially kill plasmid-carrying bacteria.
source: Our results suggest that these responses can be exploited to preferentially kill plasmid-carrying bacteria.
evidence: This is characterized as a suggestion based on experimental results, indicating inference from data.

claim: All six plasmids carried important ß-lactamase genes, including extended-spectrum ß-lactamases (ESBLs), AmpC-type ß-lactamases, or carbapenemases.
source: All plasmids carried important ß-lactamase genes, including extended-spectrum ß-lactamases (ESBLs), AmpC-type ß-lactamases, or carbapenemases, as well as other relevant ABR genes (Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing plasmid characteristics.

claim: The six plasmids belonged to a broad range of incompatibility groups.
source: These plasmids belonged to a broad range of incompatibility groups, covered a range of different sizes, included conjugative and non-conjugative specimens, and produced variable fitness effects, ranging from 10% to 27% reductions in relative fitness, when introduced into E. coli MG1655 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and experimental characterization.

claim: The six plasmids covered a range of different sizes.
source: These plasmids belonged to a broad range of incompatibility groups, covered a range of different sizes, included conjugative and non-conjugative specimens, and produced variable fitness effects, ranging from 10% to 27% reductions in relative fitness, when introduced into E. coli MG1655 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1A and Table 1 showing plasmid sizes.

claim: The six plasmids included conjugative and non-conjugative specimens.
source: These plasmids belonged to a broad range of incompatibility groups, covered a range of different sizes, included conjugative and non-conjugative specimens, and produced variable fitness effects, ranging from 10% to 27% reductions in relative fitness, when introduced into E. coli MG1655 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by reference to Table 1 showing mobility characteristics.

claim: The six plasmids produced variable fitness effects, ranging from 10% to 27% reductions in relative fitness, when introduced into E. coli MG1655.
source: These plasmids belonged to a broad range of incompatibility groups, covered a range of different sizes, included conjugative and non-conjugative specimens, and produced variable fitness effects, ranging from 10% to 27% reductions in relative fitness, when introduced into E. coli MG1655 (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A from competition assays.

claim: All plasmids conferred resistance to ß-lactam antibiotics.
source: As expected from their genetic content, all plasmids conferred resistance to ß-lactam antibiotics and most of them conferred additional resistance to other antibiotics from unrelated families (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Most of the six plasmids conferred additional resistance to other antibiotics from unrelated families.
source: As expected from their genetic content, all plasmids conferred resistance to ß-lactam antibiotics and most of them conferred additional resistance to other antibiotics from unrelated families (Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Supported by MIC data shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: Seven CS instances producing a consistent ≥2-fold reduction in antibiotic susceptibility were identified.
source: This led to the identification of seven CS instances producing a consistent ≥2-fold reduction in antibiotic susceptibility, of which six showed significant reductions in antibiotic susceptibility (pOXA-48–azithromycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, pCF12–kanamycin, pKAZ3–kanamycin, and pKAZ3-gentamicin; Mann-Whitney U test; p<0.015 in all cases; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by MIC determinations and statistical analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Six CS instances showed significant reductions in antibiotic susceptibility: pOXA-48–azithromycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, pCF12–kanamycin, pKAZ3–kanamycin, and pKAZ3-gentamicin.
source: This led to the identification of seven CS instances producing a consistent ≥2-fold reduction in antibiotic susceptibility, of which six showed significant reductions in antibiotic susceptibility (pOXA-48–azithromycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, pCF12–kanamycin, pKAZ3–kanamycin, and pKAZ3-gentamicin; Mann-Whitney U test; p<0.015 in all cases; Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by MIC determinations with statistical significance testing (Mann-Whitney U test; p<0.015).

claim: CS to tetracycline elicited by pKA2Q did not reach statistical significance.
source: Of note, CS to tetracycline elicited by pKA2Q did not reach statistical significance (Mann-Whitney U test; p=0.2), yet we decided to maintain it for subsequent analysis.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MIC data (Mann-Whitney U test; p=0.2).

claim: Six of the seven CS instances initially identified were validated with at least one additional method (growth curves or disk-diffusion assays).
source: Overall, six of the seven CS instances initially identified were validated with at least one of the additional methods (growth curves or disk-diffusion assays), and four of them showed full agreement across all three methods.
evidence: This is a summary of validation experiments using multiple methodologies.

claim: Four CS instances showed full agreement across all three methods (MIC, growth curves, and disk-diffusion assays).
source: Overall, six of the seven CS instances initially identified were validated with at least one of the additional methods (growth curves or disk-diffusion assays), and four of them showed full agreement across all three methods.
evidence: This is a summary of validation experiments using multiple methodologies.

claim: ABR plasmids produce moderate but significant CS to different antibiotics, comparable to that generated by ABR chromosomal mutations in E. coli.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that ABR plasmids produce moderate but significant CS to different antibiotics, comparable to that generated by ABR chromosomal mutations in E. coli (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Lázár et al., 2013; Podnecky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and compared to prior studies via citation.

claim: The success and applicability of CS-informed therapeutic strategies are crucially dependent on the conservation of CS across diverse genetic contexts.
source: The success and applicability of CS-informed therapeutic strategies are crucially dependent on the conservation of CS across diverse genetic contexts (Podnecky et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research establishing this principle.

claim: pOXA-48 confers resistance to last-resort carbapenem antibiotics.
source: To address the phylogenetic preservation of plasmid-induced CS, we focused on the plasmid pOXA-48, which confers resistance to last-resort carbapenem antibiotics, and whose prevalence in clinical settings is rising alarmingly (David et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pOXA-48 supported by citation.

claim: The prevalence of pOXA-48 in clinical settings is rising alarmingly.
source: To address the phylogenetic preservation of plasmid-induced CS, we focused on the plasmid pOXA-48, which confers resistance to last-resort carbapenem antibiotics, and whose prevalence in clinical settings is rising alarmingly (David et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CS to azithromycin mediated by pOXA-48 showed a striking degree of conservation across E. coli strains, with eight out of nine plasmid-carriers showing significantly higher susceptibility than their plasmid-free counterparts.
source: CS to azithromycin showed a striking degree of conservation across the strains, with eight out of nine plasmid-carriers showing significantly higher susceptibility than their plasmid-free counterparts.
evidence: Supported by disk-diffusion assay data across nine diverse E. coli clinical isolates shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CS to colistin mediated by pOXA-48 was conserved in only two of the nine tested E. coli strains.
source: In contrast, CS to colistin was conserved in only two of the tested strains (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by disk-diffusion assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All nine tested E. coli strains showed CS responses to at least one antibiotic when carrying pOXA-48.
source: Nevertheless, all strains showed CS responses to at least one antibiotic, suggesting that pOXA-48 elicits CS responses that could potentially be exploited therapeutically.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from disk-diffusion assays.

claim: pOXA-48 elicits CS responses that could potentially be exploited therapeutically.
source: Nevertheless, all strains showed CS responses to at least one antibiotic, suggesting that pOXA-48 elicits CS responses that could potentially be exploited therapeutically.
evidence: This is characterized as a suggestion based on experimental data, indicating inference and speculation.

claim: In 11 of the 20 possible strain-treatment combinations, pOXA-48–carrying populations showed higher mortality rates than their plasmid-free counterparts.
source: In 11 of the 20 possible strain-treatment combinations, pOXA-48–carrying populations showed higher mortality rates than their plasmid-free counterparts (Figure 3; log-rank test p<0.001 in all cases).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 3 with statistical analysis (log-rank test p<0.001).

claim: The mortality patterns observed were consistent with the CS patterns obtained in the disk-diffusion technique.
source: Nevertheless, the mortality patterns observed were consistent with the CS patterns obtained in the disk-diffusion technique (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing data from two different experimental approaches.

claim: Plasmid-carrying MG1655 and Ec18 strains, which show CS to both antibiotics, exhibited significant reductions in survival in all treatments.
source: For instance, plasmid-carrying MG1655 and Ec18 strains, which show CS to both antibiotics, exhibited significant reductions in survival in all treatments.
evidence: Supported by survival curve data from antibiotic treatment experiments.

claim: For strain Ec10, which shows CS exclusively to colistin, selective killing was observed only when the treatment included colistin as the first antibiotic.
source: In contrast, for strain Ec10, which shows CS exclusively to colistin, selective killing was observed only when the treatment included colistin as the first antibiotic (Col→ Col or Col→ Azi).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data from antibiotic treatment experiments.

claim: The molecular basis of plasmid-associated CS is currently unknown.
source: However, the molecular basis of plasmid-associated CS is currently unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The feasibility of rational broad-spectrum anti-plasmid strategies will depend on gaining comprehensive knowledge about the molecular mechanisms that increase antibiotic susceptibility upon plasmid acquisition.
source: The feasibility of rational broad-spectrum anti-plasmid strategies will depend on gaining comprehensive knowledge about the molecular mechanisms that increase antibiotic susceptibility upon plasmid acquisition.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research needs and applications.

claim: Colistin and azithromycin may be valuable antibiotics for the treatment of pOXA-48–carrying enterobacteria.
source: In this regard, our results suggest that colistin and azithromycin may be valuable antibiotics for the treatment of pOXA-48–carrying enterobacteria.
evidence: This is characterized as a suggestion based on experimental results, indicating inference and speculation.

claim: Both colistin and azithromycin are already used to treat enterobacterial infections.
source: Both antibiotics are already used to treat enterobacterial infections (Lübbert, 2016; Morrill et al., 2015), and colistin in particular is currently used as a last resort antibiotic against carbapenem-resistant enterobacteria (Rodriguez-Baño et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior clinical research.

claim: Colistin is currently used as a last resort antibiotic against carbapenem-resistant enterobacteria.
source: Both antibiotics are already used to treat enterobacterial infections (Lübbert, 2016; Morrill et al., 2015), and colistin in particular is currently used as a last resort antibiotic against carbapenem-resistant enterobacteria (Rodriguez-Baño et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to clinical practice guidelines.

claim: Sequential treatments offer a promising strategy, as they better exploit evolutionary trade-offs (such as CS) to constraint ABR development.
source: Sequential treatments offer a promising strategy, as they better exploit evolutionary trade-offs (such as CS) to constraint ABR development (Kim et al., 2014; Roemhild and Schulenburg, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on treatment strategies.

claim: Combination therapies might provide a valuable strategy as long as both antibiotics act synergistically to inhibit bacterial growth.
source: Combination therapies might also provide a valuable strategy as long as both antibiotics act synergistically to inhibit bacterial growth (Tamma et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research, characterized as speculative ('might').

claim: pOXA-48_K8 is a pOXA-48-like plasmid that shares a 100% coverage and >99% identity with the first described pOXA-48 plasmid.
source: pOXA-48_K8 is a pOXA-48-like plasmid that shares a 100% coverage and >99% identity with the first described pOXA-48 plasmid (León-Sampedro et al., 2020; Poirel et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison data and citations to prior characterization.

claim: Analysis of the area under the growth curve confirmed significant plasmid-mediated CS effects at different antibiotic concentrations for six combinations: pOXA-48–azithromycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, pCF12–kanamycin, pKAZ3–kanamycin, and pKA2Q–tetracycline.
source: Analysis of the area under the growth curve, which integrates all growth parameters (maximum growth rate, lag duration and carrying capacity) (DelaFuente et al., 2020), confirmed significant plasmid-mediated CS effects at different antibiotic concentrations for six of the combinations (pOXA-48–azithromycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, pCF12–kanamycin, pKAZ3–kanamycin, and pKA2Q–tetracycline; Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: Supported by growth curve analysis shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The disk-diffusion results showed a general trend toward an increased diameter of the antibiotic inhibition zone in plasmid-carrying strains compared with plasmid-free MG1655.
source: The disk-diffusion results largely agreed with the MIC and growth-curve data, showing a general trend toward an increased diameter of the antibiotic inhibition zone in plasmid-carrying strains compared with plasmid-free MG1655 (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by disk-diffusion assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Disk-diffusion assays showed statistically significant differences for pCF12–kanamycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, and pKA2Q–tetracycline.
source: These differences were statistically significant for pCF12–kanamycin, pCF12–azithromycin, pOXA-48–azithromycin, pOXA-48–colistin, and pKA2Q–tetracycline (unpaired t-test with Welch's correction; p<0.044 in all cases).
evidence: Supported by disk-diffusion assay data with statistical analysis (unpaired t-test with Welch's correction; p<0.044).

claim: The disk-diffusion technique is appropriate for screening CS responses in large strain collections.
source: The disk-diffusion assays produced notably robust results with minimum hands-on time, suggesting that this technique is appropriate for screening CS responses in large strain collections.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results regarding the utility of the method.

claim: No significant chromosomal mutations accumulated during the process of plasmid acquisition in MG1655 derivatives.
source: Strain constructions were verified by assessing that the ABR profile of plasmid-bearing MG1655 matched the expected resistance of the plasmid (Supplementary file 1A) and by sequencing the complete genomes of transconjugant clones, which also revealed that no significant chromosomal mutations accumulated during the process of plasmid acquisition (0–2 mutations between plasmid-carrying and plasmid-free complete genomes, see Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data showing 0-2 mutations between plasmid-carrying and plasmid-free genomes.

claim: Plasmid loss in plasmid-carrying strains is negligible under the experimental conditions used.
source: We performed control experiments mimicking the growth conditions of the competition experiments to ensure that plasmid loss in plasmid-carrying strains is negligible.
evidence: Supported by control experiments performed to validate the competition assay methodology.

claim: Plasmid conjugation under the experimental conditions used for the competition assays does not significantly affect relative fitness determinations.
source: Moreover, previous results indicated that plasmid conjugation under the experimental conditions used for the competition assays do not significantly affect relative fitness determinations (Alonso-del Valle et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research validating the methodology.

claim: The antibiotic concentrations used (8 mg/L azithromycin and 4 mg/L colistin) are within the range of clinical breakpoints determined by EUCAST.
source: Although we used non-standardized media and culture conditions, these concentrations are within the range of clinical breakpoints determined by EUCAST, which are 16 µg/ml for azithromycin (clinical breakpoints only available for Salmonella typhi and Shigella spp) and 2 µg/ml for colistin (according to EUCAST clinical breakpoints version eleven; EUCAST, 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison to established clinical standards supported by citation to EUCAST guidelines.

claim: The physiological alterations produced upon acquisition of ABR plasmids might lead to exploitable CS responses.
source: We reasoned that the physiological alterations produced upon acquisition of ABR plasmids might lead to exploitable CS responses.
evidence: This is the hypothesis that motivated the study, based on inference from prior knowledge.

claim: This is the first analysis of CS associated with the acquisition of complete ABR plasmids.
source: Here, we report the first analysis of CS associated with the acquisition of complete ABR plasmids, including the clinically important carbapenem-resistance conjugative plasmid pOXA-48.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on review of existing literature.

claim: Plasmid pCEMR is a derivative of pEncl-30969cz in which a spontaneous deletion of ~19 kb had occurred.
source: Plasmid pCEMR is a derivative of pEncl-30969cz in which a spontaneous deletion of ~19 kb had occurred (Acc. No. MT720903).
evidence: This describes the origin and characteristics of plasmid pCEMR based on sequence analysis.

claim: Plasmids pOXA-48_K8 and pCF12 were isolated from rectal swabs of patients hospitalized in the Ramón y Cajal University Hospital in the framework of the R-GNOSIS project.
source: Plasmids pOXA-48_K8 (Acc. No. MT441554) and pCF12 (Acc. No. MT720906) were isolated from rectal swabs of patients hospitalized in the Ramón y Cajal University Hospital in the framework of the R-GNOSIS project (Hernández-García et al., 2018b).
evidence: This describes the source of the plasmids used in the study.

claim: The clinical E. coli strains used in this study were isolated during the R-GNOSIS project, which included representative ESBL-producing enterobacteria from hospitalized patients in the Ramon y Cajal University Hospital during a 2-year period.
source: The clinical E. coli strains used in this study were isolated during the R-GNOSIS project, which included representative ESBL-producing enterobacteria from hospitalized patients in the Ramon y Cajal University Hospital during a 2-year period (Hernández-García et al., 2018b; León-Sampedro et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the source of the clinical strains used in the study.
